---
title: Feature Flags
icon: Flag
description: "Ship behind a switch: boolean, string, number and JSON flags with targeting rules, per-user overrides and percentage rollouts, evaluated per request."
---

import { FlaskConical, Users, LineChart, Boxes } from 'lucide-react';

A feature flag decouples "is this code deployed" from "is this feature on". You
ship the code dark, then turn it on for yourself, then a team, then five percent
of users, then everyone, without another deploy. Applad flags live under
`/v1/flags` and share the same project scope as the rest of the platform: your
app asks "is this flag on for this user?" and gets back a value computed from the
flag's rules, overrides and rollout.

A flag has a **type** (`boolean`, `string`, `number`, or `json`), so it is not
just an on/off switch. A `string` flag can pick a variant, a `number` flag can
carry a limit, and a `json` flag can ship a whole config object. Every flag has a
**default value** that applies when no rule matches.

<Callout title="Two sides of the API">
Everyday reads use the **evaluation** endpoints, which take a flag `key` and a
context and are exposed by every SDK. **Management** (creating flags, rules and
overrides) is done from your backend or the console and addresses a flag by its
generated `$id`. This page covers both.
</Callout>

## Evaluate a flag

Evaluation is the call your app makes on every request. Pass the flag `key` and,
optionally, an evaluation **context** describing who is asking. If you omit the
`userId`, Applad fills it in from the authenticated caller.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Node.js', 'Python', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
// Client SDK: userId is taken from the signed-in session automatically.
const result = await client.flags.evaluateFlag('new-checkout', {
  email: 'ada@example.com',
  attributes: { plan: 'pro' },
});
if (result.value === true) {
  // show the new checkout
}
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Node.js">
```ts
const result = await server.flags.evaluateFlag('new-checkout', {
  userId: 'user_123',
  teamIds: ['team_42'],
  attributes: { plan: 'pro' },
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python
result = client.flags.evaluate_flag("new-checkout", {
    "userId": "user_123",
    "attributes": {"plan": "pro"},
})
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/flags/evaluate \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"key":"new-checkout","context":{"userId":"user_123","attributes":{"plan":"pro"}}}'
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Underlying route: `POST /v1/flags/evaluate`. The response is an evaluation result:

```json
{
  "key": "new-checkout",
  "value": true,
  "enabled": true,
  "ruleId": "rule_abc",
  "reason": "rule"
}
```

The `reason` tells you why you got that value:

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `override` | A per-user or per-team override matched (highest priority). |
| `rule` | A targeting rule matched (and the user fell inside its rollout). |
| `default` | The flag is on but no rule matched, so its default value applies. |
| `disabled` | The flag is turned off. You get its default value and `enabled: false`. |
| `not_found` | No flag with that key exists. You get `value: null`. |

An unknown key returns `not_found` rather than erroring, so a stale key in your
app degrades to "off" instead of throwing.

### Evaluate one, or all

There are three evaluation entry points:

| SDK method | Route | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `evaluateFlag(key, context)` | `POST /v1/flags/evaluate` | Evaluate one flag with a full context. |
| `getFlag(key)` | `GET /v1/flags/evaluate/{key}` | Evaluate one flag using just the signed-in user. |
| `getAllFlags(context)` | `POST /v1/flags/evaluate/all` | Evaluate every flag at once, returned as a map keyed by flag key. |

`getAllFlags` is what you call on app start to hydrate a whole flag set in one
round trip:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Python']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const { flags } = await client.flags.getAllFlags({ attributes: { plan: 'pro' } });
// flags['new-checkout'].value, flags['dark-mode'].value, ...
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python
res = client.flags.get_all_flags({"attributes": {"plan": "pro"}})
flags = res["flags"]
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### The evaluation context

The context is how a flag decides. Every field is optional.

| Field | Type | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `userId` | string | Overrides, `userId` conditions, and sticky rollout bucketing. Auto-filled from auth when omitted. |
| `teamIds` | string array | Team overrides and `teamId` / `teamIds` conditions. |
| `email` | string | `email` conditions. |
| `labels` | string array | `label` conditions. |
| `attributes` | object | Custom conditions, addressed as `custom.<name>` or by bare name. |

## Create a flag

The management side is done from trusted code (a server SDK or the console).
Creating a flag from HTTP lets you set its type and default value directly:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/flags \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "key": "new-checkout",
    "name": "New checkout flow",
    "type": "boolean",
    "defaultValue": false,
    "tags": ["checkout"]
  }'
```

Underlying route: `POST /v1/flags`. The response carries the flag's generated
`$id`, which the rule and override routes below address:

```json
{
  "$id": "flag_abc123",
  "key": "new-checkout",
  "name": "New checkout flow",
  "type": "boolean",
  "defaultValue": false,
  "enabled": true,
  "tags": ["checkout"],
  "rules": []
}
```

A flag defaults to `type: "boolean"` with `defaultValue: false` when you omit
them. A duplicate `key` in the same project is rejected with `409`.

The server SDKs (Node, Go, Python, Dart) also expose management helpers:
`list`, `create`, `get`, `update`, `delete` and `toggle`. These are convenience
wrappers over the routes on this page; anything they do not cover (rules,
overrides, stats) you call over HTTP.

<Callout title="Turn a flag on and off">
A flag is created **enabled**. Flip it with
`PATCH /v1/flags/{flagId}/toggle` and a body of `{"enabled": false}`. A disabled
flag short-circuits evaluation: every caller gets the default value with
`reason: "disabled"`, so an emergency kill switch is one request.
</Callout>

## Targeting rules

A rule turns a flag on for a subset of users. Each rule has a **type**, a list of
**conditions** (all of which must match, so conditions are AND-ed), a **value**
to return when it matches, and a **rollout percentage**. Rules are evaluated in
creation order, and the first one that matches wins.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/flags/<flagId>/rules \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "type": "attribute",
    "conditions": [
      { "attribute": "custom.plan", "operator": "eq", "value": "pro" }
    ],
    "value": true,
    "rolloutPct": 50
  }'
```

Underlying route: `POST /v1/flags/{flagId}/rules`. List and delete them with
`GET /v1/flags/{flagId}/rules` and
`DELETE /v1/flags/{flagId}/rules/{ruleId}`.

A condition's `operator` is one of:

| Operator | Matches when the attribute |
| --- | --- |
| `eq` / `neq` | equals / does not equal the value |
| `contains` | contains the value as a substring |
| `starts_with` / `ends_with` | has the value as a prefix / suffix |
| `in` / `not_in` | is (not) one of a comma-separated or array value |
| `gt` / `lt` | sorts after / before the value |
| `exists` / `not_exists` | is present / absent |

The `attribute` resolves against the context: `userId`, `email`, `teamId`,
`teamIds`, `label`, or a custom attribute as `custom.<name>` (a bare name is
also looked up in `attributes`). Comparisons are string-based, so `gt` and `lt`
compare lexically.

### Percentage rollout

Set `rolloutPct` below 100 to give a rule to only a slice of the users it would
otherwise match. Bucketing is **sticky**: Applad hashes the flag key together
with the user id, so the same user always lands in or out of the same rollout,
and raising the percentage only ever adds users. A rule with no matchable user
id treats an anonymous caller as a stable bucket named `anonymous`.

## Per-user and per-team overrides

An override pins a flag to an exact value for one user or team, ahead of every
rule. Use it to force a feature on for a beta tester or off for a customer who
hit a bug.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/flags/<flagId>/overrides \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "targetType": "user", "targetId": "user_123", "value": true }'
```

Routes: `POST` / `GET /v1/flags/{flagId}/overrides` and
`DELETE /v1/flags/{flagId}/overrides/{targetType}/{targetId}`. `targetType` is
`user` or `team`. During evaluation a user override is checked first, then any
team override for a team in `teamIds`, before any rule runs.

## Evaluation stats

Each evaluation is recorded, and
`GET /v1/flags/{flagId}/stats` returns a rollup: total evaluations, distinct
users, and the distribution of returned values.

```json
{
  "totalEvaluations": 10432,
  "uniqueUsers": 811,
  "distribution": [
    { "value": true, "count": 6120 },
    { "value": false, "count": 4312 }
  ]
}
```

This is enough to confirm a rollout is reaching roughly the share of users you
expect before you widen it.
